claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 can initially exist in a high-temperature BCC state.
Phase stability in the high-temperature BCC state is controlled by a balance between thermodynamic driving forces for elemental partitioning and kinetic barriers to atomic diffusion.
Al segregation lowers the alloy's free energy.
The high-temperature BCC state is thermodynamically unstable or metastable under the relevant post-processing conditions.
Rapid cooling and limited diffusion can kinetically preserve the metastable BCC state.
Slower cooling or prolonged annealing permits Al redistribution.
Al redistribution leads to phase separation or transformation.
Changing annealing temperature and hold time controls the extent of elemental diffusion, especially Al diffusion.
Brief annealing holds produce less diffusion than extended holds under otherwise controlled conditions.
Al partitions at grain boundaries or incipient secondary-phase regions during phase evolution.
Local Al partitioning changes local free energy and thereby mediates phase evolution.
Chemical-potential differences, particularly those associated with Al, provide the thermodynamic driving force for segregation.
The kinetic barrier to diffusion counteracts the thermodynamic instability.
Al segregation locally lowers free energy and drives formation of more thermodynamically stable secondary phases.
Longer anneals at sub-critical temperatures will produce detectable Al enrichment.
Longer anneals at sub-critical temperatures will produce secondary phases in addition to or instead of BCC.
Rapidly quenched samples will retain a more compositionally homogeneous BCC structure than long-annealed samples.
Ordering transformations that require little elemental migration could provide an alternative transformation pathway outside the proposed mechanism.
Minor impurities or processing variations can shift the temperature and time regimes in which thermodynamic and kinetic competition controls phase stability.
